The '''South Texas Family Residential Center''' (also called Dilley Immigration Processing Center) is an immigrant detention center in [[Dilley, Texas]]. First opened in December 2014, under [[Barack Obama]], it has a capacity of 2,400 and is intended to detain mainly women and children from Central America.<ref name="auto1">{{cite news|url=http://www.cbsnews.com/news/south-texas-immigration-detention-center-set-to-open/|title=South Texas immigration detention center set to open|date=15 December 2014|work=CBS News|access-date=19 December 2014|agency=Associated Press}}</ref> [[United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement]] (ICE) closed the detention center in June 2024, citing cost savings to add more beds in other facilities as the [[Presidency of Joe Biden|Biden administration]] implemented new border restrictions. It reopened the following year, in
2025.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2024-06-10 |title=US to close costly Texas immigration detention center and reroute funds |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/us/us-close-costly-texas-immigration-detention-center-reroute-funds-2024-06-10/ |access-date=2024-06-11 |website=Reuters |language=en-US|last=Hesson|first=Ted}}</ref> 

In 2025, [[CoreCivic]] announced a new contract with ICE to reopen the facility as the '''Dilley Immigration Processing Center'''.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Hurwitz |first=Sophie |title=Private prison companies set to make billions reopening jails for ICE |url=https://www.motherjones.com/politics/2025/03/private-prison-mass-deportation-trump-billions-geogroup-corecivic-ice/ |access-date=2025-03-06 |magazine=Mother Jones |language=en-US|date=March 6, 2025}}</ref> ICE awarded the CoreCivic and [[Target Hospitality]] a 5-year contract in 2025, aiming to immediately resume operations.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-03-05 |title=CoreCivic Announces Resumption of Operations at South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas |url=https://ir.corecivic.com/news-releases/news-release-details/corecivic-announces-resumption-operations-south-texas-family|access-date=2025-08-15 |website=CoreCivic |language=en-US}}</ref> CoreCivic receives $160 million annually to operate the facility.<ref>{{Cite news| last = Serrano| first = Alejandro| title = South Texas immigration detention center to reopen| work = The Texas Tribune| access-date = 2026-01-27| date = 2025-03-06| url = https://www.texastribune.org/2025/03/06/texas-dilley-immigration-detention-center-families-reopen/}}</ref> As of 2025, the facility was exceeded in total capacity and average daily population by some other detention centers, including [[Camp East Montana]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite news| issn = 0190-8286| last1 = MacMillan| first1 = Douglas| last2 = Kirkpatrick| first2 = N.| last3 = Sidhom| first3 = Lydia| title = ICE documents reveal plan to double immigrant detention space this year| newspaper = The Washington Post| access-date = 2026-01-27| date = 2025-08-15| url = https://www.washingtonpost.com/immigration/2025/08/15/ice-documents-reveal-plan-double-immigrant-detention-space-this-year/}}</ref>

A 2025 ICE planning document described the possible construction of a 250-person "soft-sided" detention center at the site.<ref name=":1" />

==Location and description==
[[File:TXMap-doton-Dilley.PNG|thumbnail|left|Approximate location in [[Texas]]]]
The site is located approximately {{convert|100| miles}} north of the [[Rio Grande]] and {{convert|70| miles}} southwest of San Antonio, southwest of [[Dilley, Texas]], in Frio County.<ref name="auto1"/> The address is 300 El Rancho Way, Dilley, Texas, United States, zip code 78017.<ref name="auto">{{cite web|url=http://www.corecivic.com/facilities/south-texas-family-residential-center|title=South Texas Family Residential Center|access-date=2025-03-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250319174903/http://www.corecivic.com/facilities/south-texas-family-residential-center|archive-date=2025-03-19}}</ref>

The {{convert|50|acre||adj=mid| site}} contains 80 small, tan-colored, two-bedroom, one-bathroom cottages for the families. The cottages can house up to eight people and contain bunk beds as well as baby cribs. They also have a flat-screen television. There is a kitchen, but cooking is not allowed in order to prevent fires. The cottages are connected by dirt roads.

There are also recreational and medical facilities, a school, trailer classrooms, a library, a basketball court, playgrounds, and email access. A cafeteria is open for 12 hours a day, but snacks can be obtained at any hour.<ref name="auto1"/>

The site was formerly a camp used by oilfield workers.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.thedailybeast.com/cheats/2014/12/16/largest-detention-center-in-u-s-opens.html|title=Largest Detention Center in U.S. Opens|work=The Daily Beast|access-date=19 December 2014|date=Dec 16, 2014}}</ref>
==Detainees==
The South Texas Family Residential Center was at first only able to accommodate 480 people when the first group of residents arrive in December 2014 from a Border Patrol training camp located in [[Artesia, New Mexico]]. Capacity expanded over the following months as construction and staffing continued, reaching up to 2,400 residents by mid-2015, with a staff of around 600.<ref name="auto1"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://spectrumlocalnews.com/us/snplus/news/2015/05/8/south-texas-family-residential-center-adding-beds|title=South Texas Family Residential Center Adding Beds|access-date=28 Jan 2026|date=May 8, 2015|website=Spectrum Local News|last=Salazar|first=John}}</ref> It is intended to detain mostly women and children from Central America.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/op-ed/la-oe-garbus-asylum-women-honduras-central-america-20190324-story.html|title=Fleeing threats to her children, a Honduran woman now faces a tough fight for asylum|last=Garbus|first=Martin|date=March 24, 2019|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=26 March 2019}}</ref>

On June 12, 2015, it was reported that the facility was holding 1,735 people, approximately 1,000 of whom were children.<ref name="LAT 2015-06-25">{{cite news|url=https://www.latimes.com/nation/la-na-dilley-detention-20150625-story.html|title=Immigrant families in detention: A look inside one holding center|newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]]|first=Molly|last=Hennessy-Fiske|date=June 25, 2019|access-date=26 March 2019}}</ref> [[CoreCivic]], previously called "Corrections Corporation of America," sought a license in 2016 to operate the facility as a General Residential Operation but litigation was brought by [[Texas RioGrande Legal Aid]] on behalf of Grassroots Leadership and the detainees themselves to block the licensing by the [[Texas Department of Family and Protective Services]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.texasobserver.org/immigrant-family-detention-license-hold/|title=Judge Halts Child Care License for Dilley Detention Center|date=2 June 2016|work=The Texas Observer|access-date=26 March 2019|last=Garcia-Ditta|first=Alexa}}</ref> In filings dated September 30, 2018, the operator stated that the property was 100% full. By April 2019, there were 499 women and children in the facility.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.kqed.org/news/11740058/detention-beds-for-immigrant-families-nearly-empty-amid-surge-in-border-crossings|title=Detention Beds for Immigrant Families Nearly Empty Amid Surge in Border Crossings|last=Small|first=Julie|date=2019-04-13|website=KQED|language=en-us|access-date=2019-04-14|df=mdy-all}}</ref> 

In January 2026, a five-year-old [[Liam Conejo Ramos]] and his father were brought to the facility. The child's detention had attracted media attention and public outrage after photos of the child being detained in a bunny hat and [[Spider-Man|Spider-man]] backpack circulated.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-01-23 |title=Pressure mounts for release of 5-year-old held at South Texas family detention center; DHS defends ICE actions |url=https://www.tpr.org/border-immigration/2026-01-23/headline-pressure-mounts-for-release-of-five-year-old-held-at-south-texas-family-detention-center-as-dhs-disputes-some-accounts |website=Texas Public Radio |language=en}}</ref> On January 24, dozens of detained children staged a demonstration in the detention center, shouting "{{Lang|es|Libertad}}" (Spanish for "Freedom").<ref>{{Cite web |last=Davies |first=David Martin |date=2026-01-25 |title=Protest breaks out at Dilley immigration detention facility holding 5-year-old Liam Ramos |url=https://www.tpr.org/border-immigration/2026-01-24/protest-breaks-out-at-dilley-immigration-detention-facility-holding-5-year-old-liam-ramos |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=Texas Public Radio |language=en}}</ref>

Conejo Ramos's detention brought widespread public attention to the unsanitary conditions of the facility. His health deteriorated quickly due to a lack of medical care and unsafe food and water.<ref>{{Cite web|title=5-Year-Old in ICE Detention Is Sick, Says Top School Official|url=https://www.huffpost.com/entry/liam-conejo-ramos-sick-ice-detention_n_696fd209e4b0559a85915488|website=HuffPost|date=2026-01-28|access-date=2026-01-30|language=en|last=Bendery|first=Jennifer}}</ref> A judge ordered his release along with his father, and the same weekend that they were released, ICE locked down the facility and announced that cases of measles were spreading there.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Montoya-Galvez |first=Camilo |date=2026-02-01 |title=ICE halts "all movement" at Texas detention facility due to measles infections |url=https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ice-dilley-center-texas-measles-cases/ |access-date=2026-02-02 |website=CBS News |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Administration==
The facility opened in 2014 and is operated mainly by [[CoreCivic]] and [[Target Hospitality]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-usa-texas-immigration-idUSKBN0JT2H320141215|title=Largest family detention center for immigrants opens in Texas|work=Reuters|access-date=19 December 2014|last=Forsyth|first=Jim|date=December 15, 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author=Roy |first=Anusha Ghosh |date=15 December 2014 |title=New residential immigration center makes history |url=http://www.kens5.com/story/news/local/2014/12/15/immigration-homeland-security-dilley-san-antonio/20455429/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150630014318/http://www.kens5.com/story/news/local/2014/12/15/immigration-homeland-security-dilley-san-antonio/20455429/ |archive-date=2015-06-30 |access-date=19 December 2014|work=KENS5}}</ref> The facility was shut down in June 2024.<ref name=":0" />

== Public reactions ==
At the end of January 2026, several protests broke out around the facilities following reports of mistreatment of immigrants after reports from Eric Lee's attorney investigating ICE procedures, citing sounds of children crying and screaming after being detained.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-01-25 |title=Immigrant families protest at Texas facility housing 5-year-old boy, father detained in Minnesota |url=https://apnews.com/article/texas-immigration-detention-7fa98244c1b0245deb4462e9dc25292f |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=McNeel |first=Bekah Stolhandske |date=2026-01-29 |title=All Eyes on Dilley: 'It's Worse Than Anybody Thinks' |url=https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/dilley-detention-jasmine-crockett-joaquin-castro/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260205055443/https://www.texasmonthly.com/news-politics/dilley-detention-jasmine-crockett-joaquin-castro/ |archive-date=2026-02-05 |access-date=2026-02-12 |work=Texas Monthly |language=en-US|url-status=live}}</ref>

On January 28, 2026, DPS troopers arrived to control part of the protests around the camp, where agents used tear gas on several demonstrators who were protesting ICE's detention of children.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Whartnaby |first=Taylor |date=2026-01-28 |title=Protestors outside Texas ICE detention facility met with tear gas in clash |url=https://katv.com/news/nation-world/protestors-outside-dilley-ice-detention-facility-met-with-tear-gas-in-clash-with-agents |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=KATV |language=en|last2=Warner|first2=Jessica}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Aguirre |title=Chemical irritant thrown at Dilley detention center protestors |url=https://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local/article/dilley-texas-detention-center-protest-21320608.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260131162116/https://www.mysanantonio.com/news/local/article/dilley-texas-detention-center-protest-21320608.php |archive-date=2026-01-31 |access-date=2026-02-12 |work=MySA |language=en|first=Priscilla|date=Jan 28, 2026|url-status=live|last2=Wright|first2=Zachary-Taylor|last3=Arévalo|first3=Dina}}</ref> DPS agents had arrested two protesters who had approached the facilities.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2026-01-28 |title=2 protesters arrested, hit by tear gas near Dilley family detention facility |url=https://www.ksat.com/news/local/2026/01/28/protesters-detained-hit-by-tear-gas-outside-dilley-family-detention-facility/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=KSAT |language=en}}</ref>

On February 9, 2026, ''ProPublica'' released a detailed investigation into the treatment of children at the South Texas Family Residential Center, where several letters in English and Spanish from immigrant children detailing their experience at the center were disclosed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Yar |first=Cengiz |date=2026-02-09 |title="I Have Been Here Too Long": Read Letters from the Children Detained at ICE's Dilley Facility |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/ice-dilley-children-letters |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=ProPublica |language=en-US|last2=Rosenberg|first2=Mica|last3=Donlan|first3=Anna|last4=Gordon|first4=Shoshana}}</ref> The disclosure of letters from immigrant children caused outrage both in Texas and in various parts of Latin America following the mistreatment allegedly suffered by children of Colombian<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-02-10 |title=Dos niñas colombianas están detenidas en centros de ICE en EE.UU. |url=https://www.lasillavacia.com/en-vivo/dos-ninas-colombianas-estan-detenidas-en-centros-de-ice-en-ee-uu/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=La Silla Vacía |language=es-CO|trans-title=Two Colombian girls are being held in ICE detention centers in the United States.}}</ref> and Venezuelan<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lapatilla |date=2026-02-09 |title=Las conmovedoras cartas de los niños venezolanos detenidos en las instalaciones de ICE en Texas |url=https://lapatilla.com/2026/02/09/las-conmovedoras-cartas-de-los-ninos-venezolanos-detenidos-en-las-instalaciones-de-ice-en-texas/ |access-date=2026-02-12 |website=LaPatilla |language=es|trans-title=The moving letters from Venezuelan children detained at ICE facilities in Texas}}</ref> origin. After the letters and artwork created by detained children spread among the public, guards at the camp seized drawing supplies, letters and drawings, and restricted access to email.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Rosenberg |first=Mica |last2=Funk |first2=McKenzie |date=2026-02-26 |title=Seized Art, Eavesdropping Guards: Parents Describe a Clampdown at Dilley Detention Center as Kids Shared Their Stories |url=https://www.propublica.org/article/dilley-detention-center-kids-art-removal |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=ProPublica |language=en-US}}</ref>

In July 2026, 110 Democratic members of Congress, sent a letter calling for the facility to be shut down.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=July 16, 2026 |title=Democrats urge DHS to shut down Dilley immigration detention center |url=https://abcnews.com/US/democrats-urge-dhs-shut-dilley-immigration-detention-center/story?id=134750983 |access-date=2026-07-29 |website=ABC News |language=en}}</ref>

In July 2026, plaintiffs filed a brief in the [[United States District Court for the Central District of California|District Court for the Central District of California]] against attorney general [[Todd Blanche]] alleging that guards routinely abuse, neglect, and torment children at the facility.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Curry Wimbish |first=Whitney |date=2026-07-20 |title=Trump Administration Routinely Violating Immigrant Children’s Rights |url=https://prospect.org/2026/07/20/trump-administration-routinely-violating-immigrant-childrens-rights/ |access-date=2026-07-29 |website=The American Prospect |language=en-US}}</ref> The brief detailed testimonies of guards physically attacking children, denying children medical care, using racist language, entering showers while teenage girls were naked, and startling them awake during the night.<ref name=":2" />

=== Protests ===
The [[detention of Liam Conejo Ramos]], a 5-year-old U.S. citizen taken into custody with his father after an immigration enforcement operation in [[Columbia Heights, Minnesota]], and subsequently held at the Dilley facility, drew national attention in January 2026.<ref name="Guardian-Liam">{{cite news |title=ICE detains five-year-old Minnesota boy arriving home, say school officials |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/jan/21/ice-arrests-five-year-old-boy-minnesota |publisher= |date=January 21, 2026 |access-date=February 25, 2026|last=Levin|first=Sam|work=[[The Guardian]]}}</ref> When news of Liam's detention reached families inside Dilley, detained women and children staged a demonstration, chanting for release and holding signs. Outside the facility, protesters gathered and state police used [[pepper spray]] on demonstrators.<ref name="AP-pepper">{{cite news |title=Police deploy chemical irritants at protesters gathered outside Texas detention center, in photos |url=https://apnews.com/photo-gallery/trump-ice-5yearold-minneapolis-liam-dilley-c58f9ef0c267f9dfaec8ef86e15dae62 |publisher= |date=January 28, 2026 |access-date=February 25, 2026|last=Gay|first=Eric|work=[[Associated Press]]}}</ref><ref name="MP-Jan2026"/>

U.S. Representative [[Joaquin Castro]] visited the facility on January 29, 2026, spending two-and-a-half hours inside and meeting with detained families, including Liam and his father. Castro described the approximately 1,100 detainees he observed, including a 2-month-old infant, as "literally being treated as prisoners."<ref name="MP-Jan2026"/> Several other children from the [[Columbia Heights, Minnesota|Columbia Heights]] school district were also taken to Dilley, and school officials reported that two brothers detained with their mother recognized a classmate in the facility cafeteria who had been missing from their school for weeks.<ref name="NYT-Feb2026">{{Cite news |date=2026-02-13 |title='I Just Want to Get Out of Here': ICE Is Detaining Hundreds of Children |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/us/migrant-children-ice-detention.html |access-date=26 February 2026  |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

Immigration attorney Eric Lee, who represents the family of Hayam El-Gamal, an Egyptian mother detained with her five children (including 5-year-old twins) for eight months at Dilley, described conditions as "an unmitigated horror show." Lee reported that one of El-Gamal's children suffered appendicitis in detention and "was left writhing on the floor of the facility screaming and in pain" before eventually being taken to urgent care.<ref name="MP-Jan2026">{{Cite web |last=Flagg |first=Anna |last2=Heffernan |first2=Shannon |date=2026-01-29 |title=Children in ICE Detention Skyrocket in Trump's Second Term |url=https://www.themarshallproject.org/2026/01/29/ice-kids-in-detention-numbers |access-date=26 February 2026  |website=The Marshall Project |language=en}}</ref>
